title: Master Shandao's Essay on Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death for Rebirth (Annotated)
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: Original title: “Master Shandao's Essay on Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death for Rebirth”

inline.s: Original title: “Master Shandao's Essay on Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death for Rebirth”
The heart of this essay, as its title says, is:
right mindfulness at the time of death for rebirth in the Pure Land.
This was taught from the golden mouth of Master Shandao, the second patriarch of the Pure Land school, who was a reappearance of Amitābha Buddha.
Whether rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss requires right mindfulness at the time of death is the watershed between the orthodox and heretical teachings of the Pure Land school
. The orthodox teaching follows the meaning of the sutras and affirms that right mindfulness at death is required; thus Master Shandao taught:
“Continuity brings rebirth.”
(See the essay
Continuity Brings Rebirth
.) Master Yongming, a reappearance of Amitābha Buddha, taught:
“Ten recitations at the time of death bring accomplishment.”
Master Yinguang, a reappearance of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, taught:

“All who recite the Buddha's name should arouse the great bodhi-mind to deliver all beings universally. Then in this present life all conditions will be smooth and favorable, and at the time of death one will be reborn with right mindfulness, leaving the stream of ordinary beings to join the assembly of sages. Relying on the Buddha's compassionate power and one's own wheel of vows, one returns to this Sahā world, manifesting bodies universally to deliver and liberate beings.”
The patriarchs of the Pure Land school throughout history have likewise taught again and again:
right mindfulness at the time of death for rebirth.
(See the essay
Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death
The heretical teaching, by contrast, violates the meaning of the sutras and denies that right mindfulness at death is required, touting:
that reciting the name guarantees rebirth, that there is no need to observe precepts, no need to cultivate merit, no need to purify one's own mind, and that even a lifetime of evil does not matter.
[Ten recitations at the time of death bring accomplishment] Master Yongming said:

“If you wish to accomplish the ten recitations at the time of death, prepare the ford and bridge beforehand, gather and merge your merits, and dedicate them to that moment; if no recitation falls short, you need have no worry.”

(Collected in the Wan Shan Tong Gui Ji.) [Prepare the ford and bridge] “Ford and bridge” means the ferry crossing and the bridge; “prepare the ford and bridge” means to make ready in advance. [Purify one's own mind] comes from the verse of the common precepts of the seven Buddhas:
“Commit no evil, practice all good, purify one's own mind — this is the teaching of all Buddhas.”

The seven Buddhas of the past all took this verse as the principle of their practice of the precepts, and so it is called the “verse of the common precepts of the seven Buddhas.” The heretical teaching's cry of “no need to observe precepts” negates “commit no evil”; its “no need to cultivate merit” negates “practice all good”; and to these it adds “no need to purify one's own mind.” Can this still be called Buddhism? [Seven Buddhas] refers to the seven Buddhas of the past, namely Vipaśyin Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and Śākyamuni Buddha.
The Master Shandao's Essay on Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death for Rebirth is now annotated as follows:

[Zhiguizi asked: Of all matters in the world, none is greater than birth and death. When one breath comes no more, one passes to the next life; with one stray thought at the end, one falls into saṃsāra. I have repeatedly received your kind instruction on the method of Buddha-recitation and rebirth, and its principle is very clear. Yet I fear that when illness comes and death arrives, my mind and consciousness will be scattered; I also worry that others may disturb my right mindfulness and cause me to forget the pure cause. I earnestly hope you will again point out the path of return
(the road home)
and show the way, so that
(so that)
I may escape the suffering of sinking and drowning.]

Zhiguizi asked: Of all matters in the world, none is greater than birth and death. When one breath comes no more, one passes to the next life; with one stray thought at the end, one falls into saṃsāra. I have repeatedly received your kind instruction on the method of Buddha-recitation and rebirth, and its
prin

fectly
clear
and plain
. But I further
fear
that when illness comes and death arrives, my mind and consciousness will be scattered, and I also
likewise

worry that others may disturb my right mindfulness and cause me to forget the pure cause. Therefore I earnestly hope you will again instruct me in the method of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, so that I may forever escape the suffering of sinking and drowning.
[The Master
(Master Shandao)

said: Excellent question! For all people who wish to be reborn in the Pure Land at the end of life, one must not fear death. Always contemplate that this body has much suffering, and that impurity and evil karma entangle it in every way. If one can cast off this defiled body and be reborn in the Pure Land, enjoying measureless happiness and liberation from the painful states of birth and death, that is the most gratifying of things — like shedding worn clothes and putting on precious robes. Therefore, simply let go of body and mind, and give rise to no clinging.]

Master Shandao answered: You have asked well! For all people who wish to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the end of life, one must not fear death. Always contemplate that this body has much suffering, and that impurity and evil karma entangle it in every way. If one can cast off this defiled body and be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, enjoying measureless happiness and liberation from the wheel of birth and death, that is the most gratifying of things — like shedding tattered clothes and putting on precious robes. Therefore, simply let go of body and mind, and give rise to no clinging to this Sahā world.

[Whenever one encounters illness, contemplate impermanence and single-mindedly await death. Admonish one's family, as well as those who tend the sick and those who come to offer greetings, that whoever comes before me should recite the Buddha's name for me, and must not speak of idle matters at hand or of the rights and wrongs of the household; nor should they offer soft words of comfort or wish me ease and happiness, for these are all empty, florid, and useless words.]

Whenever one falls ill, contemplate the impermanence of all things and single-mindedly await death (single-mindedly await the arrival of that most sacred and solemn moment of liberation). Admonish one's family, those who tend the sick, and those who come to offer greetings, that whoever comes before my bed should recite the Buddha's name for me, and must not speak of idle matters at hand or of the rights and wrongs of the household; nor should they offer soft words of comfort or wish me ease and happiness, for these are all empty, florid, and useless words.

[Impermanence] All phenomena in the world arise and perish, flow and change, and do not abide for even an instant; this is called impermanence. Impermanence is the hallmark of this Sahā world. For living beings with sentience and form (humankind among them), there is birth, aging, sickness, and death; for lifeless things — minerals, utensils, and even mountains, rivers, and the great earth — there is formation, abiding, decay, and dissolution. Through a thorough understanding of impermanence, one realizes that whatever is born must perish, whatever gathers must scatter, whatever rises must fall; all things pass away, and in a blink everything is empty. Ending birth and death then becomes the foremost matter, and one will no longer give rise to craving for pleasing things and situations, nor to aversion toward vexing ones — for craving and aversion are the very roots of the wheel of birth and death. At the same time, through a thorough understanding of impermanence, one will constantly urge oneself on: life is short and the world is fragile, so one must seize the time to practice; when one breath comes no more, one passes to the next life.

[When the illness grows grave and the end draws near, one's relatives must not shed tears or weep, nor utter sounds of sighing and regret, lest they disturb and confuse the mind and cause it to lose right mindfulness. Instead, they should all recite the Buddha's name in unison
(together)

, and only after the breath has ceased may they grieve and weep. The moment there is even the slightest longing for the world, it becomes an obstruction, and liberation cannot be attained. If one can have a person who clearly understands the Pure Land come frequently to urge and encourage, that is a tremendous good fortune. Those who follow this practice will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land, beyond all doubt.]

When the illness grows grave and the end draws near, one's relatives must not shed tears or weep, nor utter sounds of sighing and regret, lest they disturb and confuse one's mind and cause it to lose right mindfulness. Instead, they should all recite the Buddha's name in unison, and only after one's breath has ceased may they grieve and weep. For the moment there is even the slightest longing for the world, it becomes an obstruction to rebirth, and liberation cannot be attained. If one can have a person who clearly understands the Pure Land come frequently to urge and encourage, that is a tremendous good fortune. Those who follow this practice will certainly be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, beyond all doubt.

[He asked further: May one still seek medical treatment and take medicine? He answered: Seeking medical treatment and taking medicine do not conflict with this at the outset. Yet medicine can only heal illness; it cannot heal life. When life has reached its end, what can medicine do? But to kill living beings to make medicine, in order to seek ease of body — this is not permissible. I have often seen people in the world who, being ill, kept a vegetarian diet, and had only just begun to recover when the physician again prescribed wine, meat, and fish along with the medicine, and the illness returned. From this one may trustingly know that the Buddha's power can save, while wine and meat are of no benefit.]

Zhiguizi asked further: May one still seek medical treatment and take medicine? Master Shandao answered: Seeking medical treatment and taking medicine do not conflict with this at the outset of the illness. Yet medicine can only heal illness; it cannot heal life. When life has reached its end, of what use is medicine? But to kill living beings to make medicine, in order to seek ease of body — this is not permissible. I have often seen people in the world who, being ill, took up a vegetarian diet; their illness had only just begun to improve when the physician again prescribed wine, meat, and fish along with the medicine, and the illness returned. From this one may trustingly know that the Buddha's power can save, while wine and meat are of no benefit.

[He asked further: What of seeking spirits and praying for blessings? He answered: The length of a person's life is fixed at birth; how could one borrow ghosts and spirits to extend it? If, in delusion, one puts faith in evil ways and kills living beings to make offerings to ghosts and spirits, one only increases one's offenses and actually shortens one's life. When the great life has reached its end, what can little ghosts do? All is vain panic and fear, and nothing avails; one must be very careful about this. You should post this essay before your eyes where you may see it at all times, so as to avoid forgetting it in the hour of peril.]

Zhiguizi asked further: What of seeking spirits and praying for blessings? Master Shandao answered: The length of a person's life is fixed at birth; how could one possibly borrow ghosts and spirits to extend it? If, in delusion, one puts faith in evil ways and kills living beings to make offerings to ghosts and spirits, one only increases one's offenses and actually shortens one's life. When the great life has reached its end, what can little ghosts do? All is vain panic and fear, and nothing avails; one must be very careful about this. You should post this essay where it is always before your eyes, and read, recite, and comprehend it at all times, so as to avoid forgetting it when illness grows grave and the hour of peril arrives.

[He asked further: For one who has never recited the Buddha's name in ordinary life, is this method still of use? He answered: This method, used by monastics, laypeople, and those who have never recited the Buddha's name, all attain rebirth, beyond all doubt.]

Zhiguizi asked further: For one who has never recited the Buddha's name in ordinary life, is this method still of use? Master Shandao answered: This method of “right mindfulness at the time of death for rebirth” (the patient must strive to maintain the right mindfulness of Buddha-recitation at death; relatives must not weep or lament, lest they disturb the patient's right mindfulness; the timely guidance and encouragement of a good spiritual friend can help the patient raise and sustain right mindfulness at death) — used by monastics, laypeople, and those who have never recited the Buddha's name, all attain rebirth, certainly and beyond all doubt.
[I have often seen people in the world who in ordinary life recite the Buddha's name and praise him, vowing to seek rebirth in the West with great earnestness and sincerity
(earnest and sincere)

. Yet when illness arrives, they fear death again, and will not speak a word of rebirth and liberation. Only after the breath has ceased, life has ended, and the consciousness has cast itself into the realm of darkness do they begin to recite the Buddha's name and ring the bell. This is like bolting the door after the thief has gone — what does it avail
(what use is it)
? Birth and death are a grave matter; one must exert one's own strength. If one thought goes astray
(if the final thought is not right mindfulness but a deluded thought)

, one will suffer through kalpas upon kalpas — who can take one's place? Think on this! Think on this! In times of health, you should receive and uphold this method with diligence; this is the great matter of the hour of death.]

I have seen many people in the world who in ordinary life recite the Buddha's name and praise him, vowing to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss with great earnestness and sincerity. Yet when illness arrives, they fear death again, and will not speak a word of rebirth and liberation. Only after the breath has ceased, life has ended, and the consciousness has cast itself into the realm of darkness do they begin to recite the Buddha's name and ring the bell. This is like bolting the door after the thief has gone (after the thief has already carried off the goods, one bolts the door against him) — what use is it? Birth and death are a grave matter; one must practice with one's own diligence. If the final thought goes astray (if the final thought is not right mindfulness but a deluded thought), the consequence is suffering through kalpas upon kalpas — who can take one's place? Think on this deeply! Think on this deeply! Before illness has arisen, you should receive and uphold this method of “right mindfulness at the time of death for rebirth” with diligence (you must make full preparation for right mindfulness at death — that is, Master Yongming's “prepare the ford and bridge” — while also admonishing your relatives not to weep and lament at that hour; and it is even better if you can have the assistance of a good spiritual friend at the end). This is the great matter of the hour of death!
